newsitem.title: USA: UUNET traffic charges plan ends Internet free ride.
newsitem.headline: UUNET traffic charges plan ends Internet free ride.

text.p: UUNET Technologies Inc. said on Monday it will begin charging Internet service providers for transmitting data traffic if the other companies are unable to handle reciprocal traffic loads from UUNET's network.
UUNET's action marks a significant blow to the traditional free passage of Internet message traffic over the web of networks that together form the public Internet.

The plans to charge for re-transmission have stirred an outcry among some smaller Internet service providers and Net traditionalists who warn the move could lead to a Balkanization of the Internet into rival toll roads.
"The free ride is over," said Joe Bartlett, an Internet analyst at industry research firm Yankee Group." I suppose some of the smaller guys will have a tougher time because of this."

UUNET, a unit of WorldCom Inc. and a leading provider of Internet connection services to businesses, said the move was necessary due to radical changes in the economics of the Internet transmission business during the past few years.
"This is a purely economic decision," UUNET Chief Executive John Sidgmore said. "We are 100 percent in favor of interconnection and won't deny access to anyone."

UUNET's move makes the Internet access business more closely resemble the economics of the telecommunications industry, where carriers pay each other settlement fees based on the amount of traffic traveling over each other's networks.

"A few years ago all ISPs (Internet service providers) were generally the same size and used each other's infrastructures to a more or less equal extent," Sidgmore said of his company's plans to introduce the approach. "That situation no longer exists and consequently there are many cases where peering is not appropriate."
"Peering" is an arrangement where peers, or Internet service providers of similar size, route each others' traffic to destinations on their respective networks.
Such arrangements have been based on the premise that the flow of data and use of network equipment is approximately equal in both directions, so no money changes hands.

Such free passage, begun in the days when government and university research organizations controlled and funded the Internet, was a key impetus behind the development of the Internet as an open communications tool.

This tradition has proved increasingly unwieldy in recent years as Internet traffic volumes have surged and commercial service providers have stepped in to provide much of the network infrastructure underlying the Internet.

UUNET said it has received numerous peering requests from small regional service providers which operate a network of computers used to host customer Web sites but do not own backbone tranmission equipment as companies like UUNET do.

UUNET said handling traffic from such companies require it to provide its network infrastructure free-of-charge, making no allowance for the hundreds of millions of dollars UUNET has spent to build its worldwide computer network.

The plan to charge smaller service providers is in line with efforts throughout the industry to make Internet charges more closely reflect actual costs and to eliminate various underlying subsidies that have kept Internet costs in check.

For example, Internet service providers are moving to charge customers for varying levels of service quality, based on usage and transmission speed requirements, replacing current flat-rate fees that typically run $19.95 per month.

UUNET said it would offer wholesale connection services beginning at monthly rates of $2,000 for high-speed links that transmit data at rates above 1.5 millions of bits per second. It already provides such services to hundreds of Internet service providers.

Industry analysts believe UUNET's actions reflect growing consolidation pressures in the highly fragmented Internet services industry and expect the introduction of such charges to leave a smaller number of larger players in its wake.

"This will likely precipitate a further shakeout in the Internet service business," said Hal Varian, an ecomomist and dean of the School of Information Systems and Management at the University of California at Berkeley. "There are more than 2,000 ISP's currently. That's about 1,500 too many," he said.
